title: Arranger versus orchestrator: radio cuts and commercial breaks
summary: By the 1930s radio dictated brief orchestrations that were cut for announcements, unlike his freer 1920s arranging.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well, we were talking about your career, and you made the point that with Goldkette and with Liz Galleat and Lynn Whiteman, you were an arranger, and later at a certain point you were an orchestrator, not an arranger. Would you elaborate on that a little bit?

Yes. During the '20s I was -- I was an arranger to set up something, maybe some sort of a style, to contribute any way I could. They were willing to accept that, and I did my work as I thought best. In other words, they gave me a tune to arrange. When the business -- when it came to 19 -- in the 1930s, middle 1930s anyway -- I was told what to do. I was told -- I was -- the radio business had developed to such an extent where your first number was almost bound to be cut. You didn't make an arrangement for it. You made an orchestration for it, and if you weren't aware of the fact that it was going to be cut, if there were -- if there was any time -- if they needed a minute, if they needed a minute and a half, it usually would go off the first number, the entrance number.
So get it over fast, make it full, get it over fast and -- and it would usually run about -- if you made it three minutes, that would give them at least a minute or so to cut.
So you were told to do these things. Or, if you weren't told, you found it out, because that's usually what

happened on a radio show.

And that's what happened when I was with the Whiteman band the second time. It happened on the Kate Smith show. It happened on most any show, on all the Shirket Shooret shows. You'd sit down and make an arrangement, what you thought -- you're just given the tune, nice tune, and you would make an arrangement that you thought, 'Well, this is going to sound pretty good, with these guys and those guys and this effect and that effect with a large orchestra, which they usually were.

You wanted to listen to it. You -- it was usually a sparkling number. So you would enter the way -- the way it -- you would start the arrangement out and make it nice and full for the first chorus, and then usually they would wave the thing down, and somebody would make an announcement about the product.

So I had that happen over some of the best arrangements that I'd thought I'd made, and then, whenever the announcement was over, they would bring it up. You didn't know where it would happen. But so long as it was enough of the orchestration there; then they would cut it or segue seg-way to the end. And they would really brutalize your arrangmeent.

If you put any time in it and wanted to make it so that it had some kind of style of sound or something like an arrangement -- so that all these things was a little expertise in radio business. This was not like going out in on the dance

hall and having them beat their feet as, you know, to the -- to the rhythm of the thing and get the good, giving some guys some good solos, some good backgrounds and that sort of thing. It was entirely different.
